name: delay-odd5
metrics: N 5 gt, min-pulse 6 gt, min-gap 5 gt
caption: A 5-tick delay in 11 blocks: the signal comes out exactly 5 ticks later on both edges, which a repeater line (even ticks only) cannot do. The input pushes a redstone block (top left) next to the middle piston and, through a repeater set to 1, makes the piston behind it push a second block next to the same piston from the other side 2 ticks later; the middle piston fires 1 tick after the first block lands (a piston always waits a tick after a block arrives), and the second block keeps it out until 2 ticks after the input falls. name: gate-and-5b-r7
metrics: function and, latency 4 gt
caption: AND with real signal inputs: a torch stands on each input block, so each goes out when its input turns on; the dust between them is then off exactly when both inputs are on, and the wall torch hanging under that dust turns it back into AND. 4 gt, 5 blocks.

name: gate-not
metrics: function not, latency 2 gt, tileable every 1 (0 0 1)
caption: NOT gate, 1 block: a wall torch hanging on the input block itself. The input powers that block, the torch goes out, and the torch is the output: lit exactly when the input is off. A row of them side by side inverts a whole bus.

name: gate-nand
metrics: function nand, latency 2 gt
caption: NAND gate, 2 blocks: a wall torch hanging on each input block, and the output lamp touching both torches. Each torch goes out when its own input is on, so the lamp stays lit unless BOTH inputs are on.

name: gate-or
metrics: function or, latency 0 gt, class instant, tileable every 2 (0 0 2)
caption: OR gate, 1 block, instant: a dust lying on input B's block points into the output, and input A's block sits right beside the output too. Either powered input block lights the output, with no delay.

name: gate-nor
metrics: function nor, latency 2 gt, tileable every 2 (0 0 2)
caption: NOR gate, 2 blocks: a dust lying on input B's block points into input A's block, so A's block is powered whenever A or B is on; the wall torch hanging on A's block is the output, lit only while both are off.

name: gate-nimply
metrics: function nimply, latency 2 gt
caption: NIMPLY gate (A and not B), 3 blocks: a subtract comparator reads input A's block behind it, and a dust lying ON input B's block sits at its side; the comparator passes A minus B, so the output lights only while A is on and B is off. B's block is the dust's floor.

name: gate-nimply-ba
metrics: function nimply-ba, latency 2 gt
caption: NIMPLY gate (B and not A), 3 blocks: the mirror of gate-nimply. A subtract comparator reads input B's block behind it, and a dust lying ON input A's block sits at its side, so the output lights only while B is on and A is off.

name: gate-imply
metrics: function imply, latency 2 gt
caption: IMPLY gate (A implies B), 2 blocks, glitch-free: the output lamp sits above a wall torch hanging on input A's block (lit while A is off) and in front of a repeater that stands ON A's block and carries input B (a repeater ignores the block under it). Torch and repeater both take 2 ticks, so switching both inputs at once never blinks the output.

name: gate-imply-ba
metrics: function imply-ba, latency 2 gt
caption: IMPLY gate (B implies A), 2 blocks, glitch-free: the mirror of gate-imply. The output lamp sits above a wall torch hanging on input B's block and in front of a repeater that stands ON B's block and carries input A; both take 2 ticks, so the output never blinks.

name: gate-xor
metrics: function xor, latency 2 gt
caption: XOR gate, 15 blocks, 2 ticks, glitch-free: a dust lies on each input block, and two subtract comparators stand in a square with them, so each dust is one comparator's back and the other's side. The comparator reading A's dust from behind has B's dust at its side and lights only when A is on alone; the other one, the mirror, lights only when B is on alone. The first points straight into the output; the second powers a block whose dust climbs over the square, across stones laid on the core, and lands on top of the output.

name: gate-xnor
metrics: function xnor, latency 4 gt
caption: XNOR gate, 17 blocks, 4 ticks: the 15-block XOR (a dust on each input block, two subtract comparators in a square with them) whose two signals meet on a stone instead of the output; a wall torch on that stone is the output, lit unless exactly one input is on.

name: d-latch-repeater
metrics: latency 4 gt, enable low
caption: D latch, 4 blocks: the data input feeds a repeater (on a stone) whose output is q, and the enable input feeds a second repeater pointing into its side. While that second repeater is on, the first is locked and holds q; while it is off, q follows d. So it is transparent while e is OFF; for a latch that follows d while e is ON, hang the 1-block NOT (a wall torch) on the enable input and let it feed the side repeater (5 blocks). Latency 4 ticks.

name: rs-dropper
metrics: latency 6 gt, tileable every 2 (0 2 0)
caption: Dropper RS latch, 4 blocks (track memory): two droppers face each other and hold one stone between them. s (next to the dropper by S) fires that dropper and the stone goes to the other one; r fires the dropper by R and it comes back; firing the empty one does nothing, so repeated s or r change nothing. A comparator on stone reads the dropper by R: q is its output (1). Latency 6 gt (dropper 4 + comparator 2). A stack of them tiles with NO gap (`tile: 0 2 0`): a column of latches costs 4 blocks per bit.

name: counter2-bulb
metrics: N 2, output level every 2 pulses, counts one pulse per N, tileable every 2 (0 2 0)
caption: Counter 2, one copper bulb, 3 blocks (track memory): the copper bulb T flip-flop seen as a counter: the input toggles the bulb, its comparator's level alternates every pulse (level style, period 2). The same build is tff-bulb, judged as a T flip-flop. A stack of them tiles with NO gap (`tile: 0 2 0`): a counter column costs 3 blocks per stage.

name: dff-lock
metrics: latency 6 gt, edge rising, setup 1 gt, hold 1 gt
caption: D flip-flop, 9 blocks: the data runs through two repeaters, and each has a lock repeater beside it (a locked repeater holds its output). The master's lock reads the clock block itself, so the first repeater follows d only while the clock is LOW; a wall torch hanging on that same clock block feeds the slave's lock, so the second repeater passes only while the clock is HIGH. On the rising edge the master freezes on d and the slave opens: q takes d exactly at the edge. No clock wiring at all: the clock block is part of the circuit.

name: dffe-lock
metrics: latency 6 gt, edge rising
caption: D flip-flop with enable, 12 blocks: the 9-block flip-flop (two repeaters with lock repeaters beside them; the master's lock reads the clock block, a wall torch on that block feeds the slave's) plus one more lock on the slave's other side, fed by a wall torch on the enable block. A repeater is locked if EITHER side is powered, so while e is off the slave stays locked through any clock edge and q holds; no AND gate is needed.

name: shift2-lock
metrics: N 2, latency 6 gt, edge rising
caption: 2-bit shift register, 27 blocks: two repeater-lock flip-flops in a row, the first stage's output feeding the second stage's data. The first stage reads the clock block directly (its master lock behind it, its slave's wall torch hanging on it); a dust on top of the clock block carries the clock round to the second stage's stone, which plays the same part for it. On each rising edge both stages shift at once.

axis: counter 100, one pulse per 200 inputs (toggles every 100: a square wave, a divider by 200)
name: counter100-items
metrics: N 100, output toggles every 100 pulses, counts one pulse per 200 inputs (toggles every 100: a square wave, a divider by 200)
caption: Counter 100, 23 blocks, with items (track memory, `mctas circuit memory items --n 100`): the output toggles once every 100 pulses, and the same 23 blocks count any N up to 576; only the number of items loaded changes. Two droppers face each other and hold 100 items between them; each pulse fires only one of them, so the pile walks from one to the other and each runs empty once every 100 pulses. A comparator reads each dropper, and the torch on its output block is lit exactly while that dropper is empty; both torches touch the copper bulb, which therefore toggles each time a dropper runs empty. The bulb is the phase: a comparator reading it powers the stone under the left dropper, which holds it (a dropper kept powered sees no new pulse), and through a dust under the right dropper switches off the torch beside it, which held the right one. The pulse reaches the right dropper through the input block on its lid and the left one through a dust on its own lid.

caption: A simple shulker box unloader: a dispenser places a full box on a hopper that empties it, and when the box is empty a piston breaks it so it drops into a second hopper. Details: a comparator reads the box through a stone; a repeater squares it and feeds a subtract comparator twice (directly on its side, 4 ticks late on its rear), which gives a 4-tick pulse only when the box runs empty. The pulse fires a sticky piston that pushes a stone into the box cell; the moving stone pushes the drop into the walled drop cell over the empties hopper, and the same pulse locks the emptying hopper so it cannot pick the box up. name: off-delay-2stage-k1

caption: Keeps the output on for 108 ticks after the input turns off (a long off-delay): a small fast loop keeps a bigger, slower loop topped up, and once the input is gone the big loop counts down; each extra pair of comparators in the big loop adds 56 ticks. Details: stage 1 is a two-comparator loop (4-tick lap) that the input holds full; once the input stops it decays 2 per lap, so its output lasts at least 28 ticks. A bubble-column elevator 10 blocks up (75 blocks) that rests when no item comes: the hopper under the input chest feeds a dropper that shoots each item into a water column over soul sand; the bubble column lifts it to the top source, under a ceiling, whose flow carries it back over the collecting hopper on the dropper's side (the items drift away from the dropper as they rise), which pushes it into the output chest. The dropper's clock runs only while the dropper holds an item: a comparator reads the dropper, and its signal reaches the sticky piston below the cell in front of it (a piston is also powered through the cell above it), which pushes an observer up beside the clock's other observer; the pair then pulses every 6 gt, and the lower one's back powers the stone above the dropper hard (the hopper beside the dropper stays unpowered). With the dropper empty the piston pulls the observer back down and the clock stops.
